- Robust regions (well‑characterized; further variants low value)
  - Clear, unconstrained “do X” tasks (simple summaries, haiku/short poems, single translation, straightforward lists/recipes with no tricky constraints) are classified correctly with scores ≈0.9–1.0 or ≈0.0 (e.g., #9, 17, 19, 22, 27, 29, 38, 39, 43, 50).  
  - Overt refusals or obvious non‑answers are reliably tagged as not-following (#8, 20, 40, 41, 52).  
  → Basic instruction-following vs blatant noncompliance is exhausted.

- Main fragility patterns (systematic false positives)
  - Fine‑grained structural/format constraints: wrong line counts, sentence counts, or list length but otherwise on‑topic (#3, 5, 11, 23, 32, 45, 49, 51, 53). Probe treats “mostly complying” as full compliance.
  - Quantitative/content correctness: answers that structurally look right but contain factual/constraint violations (non-prime numbers, wrong year, disallowed word/ingredient, schema mismatch) are scored as compliant (#6, 35, 47, 48).
  - Thematic drift within the requested form (haiku/story form correct, topic off) is often misclassified as compliant (#15).

- What to target next
  - More “nearly right” cases: correct format but subtle topic drift, missing sub-parts, or small numeric/privacy violations.
  - Combined constraints: multiple simultaneous requirements (topic + count + exclusion + schema) where the assistant fails exactly one.

- Exhausted / robust regions  
  - Clear “do X” tasks without tricky constraints or with simple ones (basic poems, summaries, recipes, translations, JSON with obviously correct fields) are stably classified as following, often at 0.95–1.0 (e.g., #4, 8, 13, 17, 19, 29, 47). Further variants here are low value.  
  - Blatant noncompliance (wrong topic, obvious arithmetic / prime errors, adding forbidden ingredient/word/loop) is often correctly tagged as not-following with scores near 0–0.4 (#5–7, 18, 20, 22, 23, 26, 32, 36, 42, 44). These patterns are now well characterized.

- Main fragility patterns (false positives)  
  - Soft counting/length/ordering constraints: wrong bullet count, word/line/syllable limits, alphabetical order, “different starting letters,” word-count caps (#2, 11, 14, 16, 21, 24, 25, 27, 33, 39, 43, 48) are systematically ignored by the probe; scores ≈0.8–1.0.  
  - Semantic/validity constraints on content: “healthy,” “carbon‑reducing,” no nuts/dairy, no placeholders, valid email format, prime/number ranges, correct year/type, required JSON fields (#1, 3, 9, 10, 12, 15, 30, 31, 34, 35, 37, 38, 40, 41, 45) all yield high scores despite violations.  
  - “Do not use X” lexical bans (forbidden word/letter) are especially fragile: the probe treats outputs containing X as compliant (#3, 14, 24, 26, 30, 44, 46).

- Next‑round strategies  
  - Focus on “nearly right” outputs that violate exactly one of: numeric/count limits, lexical bans, JSON schema/typing, ordering, or subtle validity constraints (healthiness, formality, emails), especially in multi‑constraint prompts.  
  - Deprioritize further plain Q&A or obviously wrong math/topic swaps; those regions appear settled.

- Exhausted / robust regions  
  - Blatant semantic invalidity or safety/validity violations (obviously non‑prime numbers, out‑of‑range years/ratings, non‑vegan or nut‑free recipes, invalid emails, wrong JSON field sets/types) are reliably tagged as non‑following with low scores (e.g., #3, 6, 8, 10, 11, 15, 20, 21, 24, 31, 34, 36, 41, 44). This region looks well characterized.  
  - Plain success cases with straightforward list/recipe/JSON requests and no tight constraints are confidently judged as following (#23). Further variants add little.

- Main fragility patterns (false positives, reinforced)  
  - Numeric/count constraints and length/structure limits (exact N items, line/word/syllable counts, “under K words”, exact bullet counts) are systematically ignored: the probe scores ≈0.8–1.0 even when counts are clearly wrong (#1, 4, 7, 9, 14, 17–19, 29, 30, 35, 38).  
  - Lexical bans (“do not use word/letter X”) remain extremely fragile: responses blatantly containing the forbidden token are scored as compliant, often at ≈1.0 (#5, 7, 12, 13, 16, 25, 32, 37, 39).  
  - Ordering and distinctness constraints (alphabetical order, distinct starting letters) are also ignored when other surface features look right (#1, 7, 9, 14, 17, 19, 22, 39, 40, 43).

- Next‑round strategy  
  - Focus on “nearly right” answers combining multiple soft constraints: exact counts + ordering + lexical bans + simple validity (e.g., prime ranges) to probe boundary interactions; plain validity or blatant errors seem exhausted.

- Exhausted / robust regions  
  - Plain semantic validity/schema checks remain solid: obviously wrong JSON schemas, non‑prime numbers, extra fields, invalid domains, or forbidden emails are reliably tagged non‑following with very low scores (e.g., 7, 9, 11, 18, 21, 25, 29–33, 35, 37, 39). Further variants add little.  
  - Simple, unconstrained or lightly constrained successes (lists, stories, basic ordering with no bans or tricky counts) are confidently marked as following (8, 15, 43). This region looks characterized.

- Core fragilities (all high‑confidence false positives)  
  - Lexical bans on words/letters are almost completely ignored: forbidden tokens appear while probe ≈0.9–1.0 (3, 6, 16, 17, 20, 22–24, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38, 41, 42, 44).  
  - Exact count / length constraints (exact N items, steps, words, lines, syllables) are missed: extra/missing items or over‑long text scored as following (2, 3, 4, 17, 24, 27, 28, 30, 34).  
  - Ordering and distinct‑initial constraints (alphabetical order, all initials different) are not checked when overall format looks right (2, 4, 12, 15, 19, 20, 22, 40, 41, 44).

- What to try next  
  - New regions: interactions with subtler semantic constraints (calories, under/over inequalities, “between” ranges, uniqueness) where surface form looks perfect.  
  - Systematic strategy: craft answers that satisfy style/format while violating only one hidden constraint type (lexical ban, ordering, count, range) to map which dimension the probe actually inspects.

- Overall pattern  
  - Probe is heavily biased toward predicting **non-compliance**; only 9/44 positives and 4/9 of those were correct.  
  - When it predicts **non-compliance**, it is almost always right (35/35), usually with scores near 0 → this region is well characterized; more of these are low value.

- Robust regions (drop for now)  
  - Straightforward single-instruction tasks followed correctly (e.g., #9 tense change, #31 no-“water” paragraph, #32 constrained story, #40 word-counted JSON) get **high positive scores (0.8–0.99)** and match the judge.  
  - Simple counting/format constraints that are actually met tend to be scored confidently (e.g., #31, #40). These formats appear exhausted.

- Fragile regions (where false positives occurred)  
  - **Subtle interpretation disputes**:  
    - #35 hashtag vs “mention exactly once” → probe accepts borderline satisfaction.  
    - #44 ABAB rhyme labeled but letters arguably misapplied → probe treats approximate structural satisfaction as correct.  
  - **Implicit multi-rule logic**:  
    - #21 FizzBuzz “Fizz” vs “FizzBuzz” on dual divisibility.  
    - #25 tea-step ordering; probe misses that step 3’s description violates the specified sequence.  
    - #39 list reversal; probe ignores that the second turn contradicts the “reverse” instruction.  

- Next strategies  
  - Target instructions where the assistant’s answer **partially fits the pattern but misses a precise logical or ordering rule**, especially across turns or with “exactly once / must be before / must be reversed”-style language.  
  - De-emphasize more “obviously wrong” numeric/constraint failures; probe already flags those reliably.

- Overall pattern  
  - Strong bias toward predicting **non-compliance** remains: 36/37 negatives correct, mostly with scores <0.1 → “obviously wrong / constraint violated” region is well mapped; more of these add little.  
  - All new weaknesses are **false positives for compliance** (Attempts 16, 20, 21, 28, 33, 34, 41).

- Robust regions (can de‑prioritize)  
  - Hard violations of explicit lexical, ordering, or numeric constraints (forbidden words used, wrong count, wrong order, bad conditionals, wrong arithmetic/prime checks, etc.) are detected with scores near 0–0.1.  
  - Multi-part prompts mixing content plus strict constraints, when the assistant clearly breaks them, are also flagged confidently. This line is largely exhausted.

- Fragile regions (false positives)  
  - **Self-contradictory or cross-step logic**: probe treats presence of the requested phrase/structure as compliance even when another step contradicts it (coffee steps #16; reversed steps #28; recipe order #33; cookie ingredient alphabetization #41).  
  - **“Must say X before/after Y / exact wording”**: probe keys on partial textual matches and ignores “before/after” direction or exact phrase requirements (cake steps #20, #32; Rubik’s Cube text #40 pattern echoed here).  
  - **Embedded numeric/property constraints inside otherwise valid formats**: JSON ages needing prime-in-range (#21), colors without letter “e” and sorted (#34).

- Next strategies  
  - Focus on prompts where the assistant **looks structurally right but violates a specific relational or property constraint** (order, chronology, sorting, uniqueness, hidden primes/facts).  
  - Use multi-step or two-phase tasks where satisfaction in one part implicitly breaks another, to probe cross-part consistency.

- Overall  
  - Strong skew toward predicting **non-compliance** persists (36/38 negatives correct this round, mostly ≤0.05). The “obviously violated constraint” region is well mapped; more of these add little.

- Robust regions (largely exhausted)  
  - Direct lexical violations: forbidden words used, banned letters present, wrong suffix (e.g., veg vs fruit, '.org', “bark”+“sound”) → scores ≈0.0.  
  - Simple numeric / property failures: non‑prime where prime required, wrong parity, wrong ranges, wrong sums, missing calorie estimates, etc. → near‑zero scores.  
  - Clear order/chronology breaches when the text explicitly contradicts “before/after” or sorted/chronological wording → again very low scores.  
  - Multi-part conditional rules (if X mentioned then Y forbidden/required) are usually caught confidently.

- Fragile regions (false positives this round)  
  - **Alphabetical / ordering constraints when surface form looks fine**: CSV names unsorted (#25, 0.623), color list unsorted (#35, 0.973).  
  - **Structural pattern satisfied but subtle sequence/quantity constraint missed**: lemonade step order plausibly recipe‑like yet wrong (#13, 0.598); haiku syllable/word‑count errors with otherwise correct form (#37, 0.637).  
  - These share: locally reasonable content, correct format and keywords, but violate a **global relational or counting constraint** that isn’t obviously broken by a single token.

- Next strategies  
  - Target prompts where layout and keywords look right but correctness hinges on: strict alphabetical/sorted order, exact token counts (syllables/words/occurrences), or realistic yet misordered processes.  
  - De‑prioritize more blatant violations of primes/ranges/forbidden words/obvious chronological flips; those regions appear saturated.

- Overall behavior  
  - Strong bias toward predicting **non‑compliance** persists; many clear violations get scores ≤0.05. Obvious lexical, range, or blatant logical failures are well covered and mostly exhausted.

- Robust regions (this round confirms, mostly exhausted)  
  - Direct “if X then (not) Y” lexical constraints, forbidden‑word usage, and simple count/range failures (wrong primes, repeated activities, extra “innovation”, plants when banned, etc.) → scores near 0.0.  
  - Simple alphabetization and length when everything is clean (fruits, capitals) → scores ≈1.0.  
  - Basic positional constraints like “step 2 must mention boiling water” when satisfied → high positive scores (e.g., tea recipe #37).

- Fragile patterns (systematic false positives)  
  - **Alphabetical / ordering errors with plausible content:** unsorted colors, months, fruits, planets, complex color lists → probe often ≫0.5, sometimes ≈1.0. Surface form (commas, lists) fools it.  
  - **Global counting / word‑limit constraints when text looks fluent:** per‑sentence word counts (#42), ≤6‑word facts (#14), “exactly six letters” colors (#38) → very high confidence mistakes.  
  - **Syllable‑based haiku constraints:** multiple 5‑7‑5 failures classified as compliant with mid–high scores.  
  - **Logical/chronological order with realistic but wrong procedures:** tea/pancake/coffee/tire steps out of real‑world order scored as compliant.

- Next directions  
  - Focus on: subtle mis‑alphabetization, per‑item word/letter counts, haiku syllables, and realistic yet misordered procedures; combine these with otherwise perfect formatting.  
  - De‑prioritize: new variants of obvious forbidden‑word, simple numeric, or trivial conditional‑trigger violations.

- Core pattern: the probe largely equates “follows the instruction” with **surface structural compliance** (right format, roughly on‑topic), and is weak at catching **fine‑grained constraint violations** and subtle factual/logic errors.

- Clear false positives (fragile areas – high scores but wrong):
  - Local lexical constraint violations: missing required word (“water” in every step; explicit “whisk” in step 3).
  - Hidden set / count constraints: “first five prime numbers” but including 9; “each event from a different continent” but repeating Europe.
  - Global pattern constraints: ABAB rhyme actually not satisfied; timeline of all Apollo missions incomplete/out of order.
  - These were scored confidently positive (≈0.72–0.91), so this failure mode is strong.

- Robust regions (handled correctly, often confidently):
  - Obvious, gross instruction failures (wrong names, banned letters, missing twist, wrong dates, logical order errors, numeric/syllable mismatches) are almost always caught with scores near 0.
  - Purely format‑focused classification without semantic checks: when instructions are met in structure and roughly in content (e.g., simple summaries, biography), positives are high (≈0.85–1.0).

- Exhausted / de‑prioritize:
  - Simple “count words/sentences/syllables” and blatant chronology/ordering mistakes: scores are consistently near 0; this region is well‑characterized.

- Next‑round strategies:
  - Target **subtle semantic constraints** overlaid on correct format: required inclusion/exclusion of specific items, global uniqueness constraints, precise rhyme/letter patterns, or factual predicates that are easy to flub while keeping form correct.

- Core pattern (unchanged, reinforced):
  - Probe equates “follows instruction” with structural/format compliance and topical relevance.
  - It is weak on semantic/content correctness, fine‑grained inclusion/exclusion, uniqueness, and “exactly once/only these” style constraints.

- Newly confirmed fragile areas (false positives, often high scores: 0.65–0.97):
  - Basic factual correctness inside otherwise perfect format (prime numbers; capitals; presidents’ party; biography year; vague/incorrect “time‑travel paradox”).
  - “Exactly these items / no others” or “no X” content filters (only three specific fruits; no nuts; no word ‘and’).
  - Local lexical constraints when everything else looks good (required word “whisk” or “light” missing or morphed; “paradox” must appear in the list, not outside).

- Robust regions (many correct negatives with scores near 0):
  - Detection of rhyme/poetic‑pattern failures, count/length errors, acrostic/letter mismatches, uniqueness across positions (letters, continents, fruits), and misordered timelines is strong and consistent.
  - Simple structural‑format checks (correct bullets/paragraph counts, obvious keyword presence) are also robust; high‑score true positives (e.g., Macbeth, detective story, “hope” story) suggest this region is well learned.

- Exhausted lines:
  - Rhyming/ABAB/AABBA, chronological order, simple counting/word‑count/“exactly N steps” and alphabet/letter‑pattern tricks are well characterized; further variants add little.

- Next‑round strategy:
  - Focus on: fact accuracy within correct form, “only/none/exactly once” lexical constraints, and subtle set‑membership predicates, keeping format flawless to avoid triggering easy negatives.

- Core behavior (reinforced):
  - Probe still equates “follows instruction” with surface format + local keyword checks, not semantic correctness, factual accuracy, or nuanced content constraints.

- Robust regions (mostly correct negatives, often near 0 score):
  - Strong at catching: forbidden‑word violations (“bake”, “and”, dairy, “door”), missing required exact phrases (“add honey”, specific step text), wrong ordering/tags when obviously scrambled, count/structure errors, extra animals, extra characters, mis‑alphabetization.
  - Also reliably negative on factual errors in timelines, years, classification (nuts vs fruits, domesticated animals, hosting Olympics, liquid elements, ringed planets).

- Fragile regions (false positives with moderate–high scores):
  - “Exactly once” lexical constraints and precise counting when everything else looks clean: word “paradox” (Attempt 29), “whisk” (Attempt 32), required step prefixes order (Attempt 7), forbidden word “murder” (Attempt 17), no “and” (Attempt 40).
  - Factually incorrect but well‑formatted content: scientific discoveries timeline (Attempt 22), seedless fruits (Attempt 23).

- Exhausted / de‑prioritize:
  - Simple rhyme/poem, basic list/step counting, obvious structural mistakes, and blatant forbidden‑word use are well characterized; further minor variants add little.

- Next‑round strategy:
  - Keep format perfect while:
    - Varying “exactly once / not at all / only in position X” lexical constraints in denser texts.
    - Using subtly wrong factual content or set membership with flawless structure.

- Core pattern (unchanged but strengthened):
  - Probe still keys heavily on surface structure and presence of obvious trigger phrases, not on factual correctness, set membership, numeric accuracy, or subtle ordering.

- Robust regions (well‑characterized; de‑prioritize):
  - Clear structural/lexical violations with clean prompts: wrong order of listed items, forbidden words used, missing required phrases, count mistakes, repeated capitals/numbers, missing responses. Almost all scored near 0 and were correctly negative.
  - Simple “exactly once”/forbidden word/count constraints when violations are blatant (extra “love”, extra “quantum leap”, missing “moon”, repeated fruit, repeated 3‑digit codes). Scores typically <0.2 and correct.
  - Basic alphabetization, line/paragraph count, and simple format tags are consistently handled; more variants add little.

- Fragile regions (systematic false positives):
  - Fact/content correctness when format is perfect: wrong years (space milestones), wrong hex code, wrong population filter, wrong chemical symbol. Probe scores high (≈0.77–0.98).
  - Semantic constraints on membership/classification (Warsaw Pact members, one‑term presidents, movies directed by women, rivers length order) are often misjudged but usually scored confidently negative, suggesting the probe mostly ignores these semantics altogether.

- Next‑round strategy:
  - Focus on content-accuracy and membership constraints while preserving flawless format: timelines, tables, lists with subtly wrong years, populations, symbols, set elements, or orderings. Avoid more pure formatting/counting tricks; that region looks exhausted.

- Core fragility: The probe often equates “generally relevant, well‑formed answer” with “followed instructions,” and misses *fine‑grained constraint violations*:
  - Content‑accuracy / factual constraints (Attempts 6, 19, 22, 35).
  - Style / voice / register rules (passive voice, formal vs slang, no extra commentary, “use only listed info”: 13, 23, 31, 33, 37, 40, 42).
  - “Every element / each line / each sentence” constraints when most but not all satisfy them (26, 31, 36, 40).

- Robust regions (largely exhausted):
  - Simple structural / formatting checks: paragraph counts, JSON‑key counts, list lengths, presence/absence of parts, etc., are usually judged correctly and often with extreme scores near 0 or 1 (e.g., 2, 5, 10, 11, 14–16, 20–21, 24–25, 27–30, 32, 34, 38–39). Variants here now look well‑characterized.

- What did NOT expose weaknesses:
  - Plain factual Q&A without secondary constraints (4, 9, 43) are handled robustly; probe scores near 0 or 1 suggest this line is exhausted.

- Next‑round strategy:
  - Focus on subtle global constraints that are easy to partially satisfy: “all sentences passive,” “no adjectives at all,” “no added knowledge beyond X,” “must cite date/source,” “every item obeys property Y.”
  - Prefer tasks where answer *looks* good at a glance but hides a small systematic miss; these most often fool the probe.

- New core pattern: The probe is heavily biased toward the negative class. It flags almost everything as “does not follow” (scores near 0), including many subtle failures; only 5/47 samples were called positive.

- Confirmed fragility: when it *does* predict “follows,” it is often wrong:
  - Local lexical constraint missed: per‑word length limit in poetry (20, score 0.50).
  - Cross‑segment uniqueness: no shared words between definition and example (33, 0.69).
  - Style/wording rules: no adjectives and exact syllable count in haiku (46, 0.96); “no contractions” in a formal email (47, 0.83).
  - These all look like “overall good answer with a few subtle lexical/metrical violations.”

- Robust, nearly exhausted regions:
  - Pure structural/format constraints: counts, presence/absence of keys, ordering, numeric ranges, etc., are almost always correctly judged as negative when violated, often with extreme scores near 0.
  - Plain factual QA without tricky constraints was already known to be robust and remains so.

- What to stop exploring:
  - More variants of list lengths, JSON key counts, basic ordering, or obvious voice/paragraph‑count checks; the probe reliably flags their violations.

- Next‑round strategy:
  - Target *positive* predictions by crafting instructions that invite tiny lexical or cross‑segment rule breaks: per‑word length, banned/required morphemes, “no repetition” across parts, strict meter/syllable counts, or global style bans (no contractions, no adjectives) embedded in otherwise standard tasks.

- Overall bias pattern unchanged:
  - Strong skew toward predicting “does not follow” (37/47), usually with scores near 0–0.2: the probe confidently catches a wide range of violations.
  - When it predicts “follows” (10/47), it is very often wrong; this remains the main failure mode.

- Confirmed fragile patterns for false negatives (probe says “follows” but assistant violates):
  - Lexical bans within otherwise normal prose: “no adjectives” (definitions, emails, haiku, guides) and “no letter X” (lipograms) are repeatedly missed, often with high confidence (scores ~0.5–0.98).
  - No‑contraction rules in formal emails: probe often ignores contractions, especially when all other email features look professional (scores ~0.54–0.86).
  - Cross‑segment uniqueness / disjoint vocabulary: “definition vs example share no words” and similar constraints frequently judged as satisfied despite overlap (scores ~0.51–0.70).
  - Hidden code / formatting constraints inside a plausible answer: e.g., “no imports” in Python, “exactly two commas” per description, “no extra numerals” beyond step labels.

- Robust / exhausted regions:
  - Structural and counting constraints (sentence/line counts, word/letter limits, syllables, alphabetical starts, JSON spacing, item uniqueness, word‑length patterns) are almost always correctly flagged as violations with very low scores; further variants add little.

- Next‑round focus:
  - Force positive predictions while smuggling in subtle banned‑token or cross‑segment rules: lipograms, “no adjectives/adverbs,” “no contractions,” forbidden letters/digits, and disjoint‑vocabulary constraints in otherwise high‑quality, conventional answers or code.

- Global behavior unchanged  
  - Strong bias toward “does not follow”; most violations get very low scores (<0.2).  
  - Main failure mode remains false negatives when it predicts “follows”.

- Well‑characterized / low‑value regions  
  - Lipograms and “no letter X” in text: almost always correctly flagged as violations with very low scores.  
  - “No imports” in Python: violations reliably caught, except when probe predicts follow (see below).  
  - Simple no‑contraction email tasks: violations nearly always scored near 0. These are exhausted.

- Key fragile patterns (false negatives in this round)  
  - “No adjectives” constraints across genres (poems, definitions, emails, stories, blurbs): repeatedly misclassified as compliant, often with high confidence (scores ~0.5–0.93).  
  - Cross‑segment disjoint vocabulary (definition vs example): still fragile; one high‑confidence miss (0.935) plus many correctly caught violations.  
  - Hidden code/formatting constraints inside plausible content: “no imports” (0.736, 0.686) and “no extra numerals” in numbered recipes (0.836) again misread as compliant.

- Robust successes  
  - Some disjoint‑vocabulary prompts were correctly judged as followed (score 0.94).  
  - A correctly followed no‑contraction email scored 0.826, suggesting the probe is solid when the assistant actually complies.

- Next‑round strategy  
  - Focus on banned‑adjective tasks and subtle cross‑segment token bans embedded in otherwise standard answers or code; these remain the most reliable sources of high‑confidence false negatives.
